explain: Sub-antimicrobial doxycycline inhibits these collagen-digesting enzymes (in part by binding their Zn<sup style="font-size:10.3168px;line-height:15.991px">2+</sup> cofactor), slowing loss of attachment around the teeth.

prompt: Xylitol gum is recommended for caries prevention. Xylitol is a sugar alcohol, not a sugar. Why do plaque bacteria make little acid from it?
choices: Xylitol is an enzyme that eats sugar
They lack the enzymes to ferment it for energy
Xylitol is a coenzyme for fluoride
answer: They lack the enzymes to ferment it for energy
hint: Bacteria need enzymes to break a sugar down.
explain: S. mutans cannot run xylitol through glycolysis the way it does sucrose, so it gets no energy and makes little acid.

prompt: Why do chlorhexidine rinse and 70% alcohol work against many kinds of bacteria at once?
choices: They competitively inhibit one bacterial enzyme
They provide a vitamin bacteria can’t use
They denature proteins and disrupt membranes, so every enzyme stops
answer: They denature proteins and disrupt membranes, so every enzyme stops
why: A competitive inhibitor targets one enzyme’s active site; disinfectants are not that specific.
hint: Specific or non-specific?
explain: Disinfectants are not specific: they unfold proteins and damage membranes. (70% alcohol beats 100% because the water helps it get into the cell.)

prompt: Bacteria in plaque use the enzyme urease: urea + H2O → 2 NH3 + CO2. What does the ammonia do in the mouth?
choices: It acts as a coenzyme for amylase
It lowers the pH and dissolves enamel
It raises the pH of plaque, which helps neutralize acid
answer: It raises the pH of plaque, which helps neutralize acid
why: NH<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">3</sub> is a base, so it raises the pH.
hint: Is NH<sub style="font-size:11.22px;line-height:17.391px">3</sub> an acid or a base?
explain: Ammonia is a base, so urease activity raises plaque pH and works against caries. (A higher pH also favors calcium phosphate deposits, so it is linked to calculus build-up.)

prompt: Articaine is an amide anesthetic, but it also has an ester group that enzymes in the blood hydrolyze right away. What does that mean for the patient?
choices: It stays in the body for days
It is cleared from the blood quickly
It can only be removed by the kidneys unchanged
answer: It is cleared from the blood quickly
hint: Blood enzymes start working on it right away.
explain: Because blood esterases start hydrolyzing articaine immediately, most of it is inactivated within minutes, which is part of why it is popular in dentistry.

prompt: Salivary peroxidase uses H2O2 to oxidize thiocyanate (SCN−) into an antibacterial product. Which enzyme class is this?
why: No bond is split by water here; one substance is oxidized while H<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub>O<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub> is reduced.
hint: The name has “oxid” hiding in it.
explain: Peroxidases catalyze redox reactions: H<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub>O<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub> is reduced and thiocyanate is oxidized to hypothiocyanite, which slows the growth of plaque bacteria.

prompt:
A patient snacks on crackers all afternoon. Starch sits in the grooves of the molars.

Which salivary enzyme starts breaking that starch down, and why does it matter for cavities?
choices: Salivary amylase: it releases sugars that plaque bacteria ferment into acid
Pepsin: it digests the enamel proteins
Lactase: it turns starch into lactose
Lipase: it releases fatty acids that dissolve enamel
answer: Salivary amylase: it releases sugars that plaque bacteria ferment into acid
why: Lipase works on fats, not starch.
hint: Which enzyme acts on starch?
explain: Amylase hydrolyzes starch into maltose and other sugars. Streptococcus mutans ferments those sugars into lactic acid, which demineralizes enamel. Sticky starchy snacks are a real caries risk.

prompt:
A patient tells the hygienist that a relative once stayed paralyzed for hours after surgery. Testing showed atypical plasma cholinesterase, a weak form of the blood enzyme that hydrolyzes ester-type local anesthetics.

Why does this matter before giving an ester-type local anesthetic?
choices: The anesthetic is broken down slowly, so it can build up and its effects last longer
The anesthetic will not work at all
The patient will need more anesthetic
Plasma cholinesterase only matters for amide anesthetics
answer: The anesthetic is broken down slowly, so it can build up and its effects last longer
why: The enzyme breaks the drug down; a weak enzyme means the drug lasts longer, not shorter.
hint: If the enzyme that removes the drug is weak, what happens to the drug?
explain: With a weak or missing enzyme, ester drugs (and the surgical relaxant succinylcholine) are hydrolyzed slowly, so blood levels stay high longer. An amide anesthetic such as lidocaine is usually chosen instead.

prompt: Lysozyme in saliva and tears breaks the glycosidic bonds in bacterial cell walls by adding water. What class of enzyme is it, and what is its job?
choices: An isomerase that makes saliva thicker
A hydrolase that helps kill bacteria
A ligase that builds bacterial cell walls
answer: A hydrolase that helps kill bacteria
why: Ligases join molecules using ATP; lysozyme breaks bonds with water.
hint: “Lyso” = split. What does it split, and with what?
explain: Lysozyme hydrolyzes the glycosidic bonds in peptidoglycan, the sugar mesh of bacterial cell walls, so bacteria burst. It is part of saliva’s built-in defense.

prompt: Nitrous oxide (N2O) inactivates vitamin B12 (cobalamin), which some enzymes need as their coenzyme. Why is long-term, unprotected N2O exposure a concern for dental staff?
choices: It can cause a vitamin B12 deficiency, with anemia and nerve damage
answer: It can cause a vitamin B12 deficiency, with anemia and nerve damage
hint: B12 deficiency causes anemia and nerve damage.
explain: N<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub>O oxidizes the cobalt in cobalamin (B12), so the enzymes that need B12 as a coenzyme stop working. Repeated exposure can cause B12-deficiency symptoms, which is why offices use scavenging systems.

prompt: Instruments are sterilized in an autoclave at 121 °C with steam. Why does this kill bacteria and viruses?
choices: The heat denatures their proteins, including all their enzymes
The steam hydrolyzes their DNA into nucleotides only
answer: The heat denatures their proteins, including all their enzymes
hint: What happens to enzymes far above their optimum temperature?
explain: At 121 °C under pressure, hydrogen bonds and other attractions holding proteins in shape break. Enzymes lose their active sites and the microbe dies.

prompt:
A farmworker in the Central Valley arrives with drooling, sweating, pinpoint pupils and muscle twitching after spraying an organophosphate insecticide. Organophosphates bond covalently to acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down the nerve signal molecule acetylcholine.

What kind of inhibition is this, and what builds up?
choices: Competitive inhibition, so acetylcholine is used up faster
Reversible inhibition, so acetylcholine levels fall
Irreversible inhibition, so acetylcholine builds up at nerve synapses
Denaturation, so H<sub style="font-size:11.5328px;line-height:17.8758px">2</sub>O<sub style="font-size:11.5328px;line-height:17.8758px">2</sub> builds up in the blood
answer: Irreversible inhibition, so acetylcholine builds up at nerve synapses
why: A covalent bond makes the inhibition irreversible, and with its breakdown enzyme blocked, acetylcholine builds up.
hint: Which enzyme normally clears acetylcholine?
explain: Organophosphates bond covalently (irreversibly) to acetylcholinesterase. Acetylcholine is not cleared, so nerves keep firing. Treatment includes atropine and pralidoxime, which can reactivate the enzyme if given early.

prompt:
A patient takes warfarin, a blood thinner. The liver needs vitamin K to make active clotting factors, and warfarin blocks the enzyme that recycles vitamin K. The patient asks if they can start eating a big spinach salad (rich in vitamin K) every day.

Why should the nurse teach them to keep vitamin K intake consistent?
choices: Vitamin K is an enzyme that digests warfarin
Warfarin blocks the enzyme that recycles vitamin K, so a big change in vitamin K changes how well the drug works
answer: Warfarin blocks the enzyme that recycles vitamin K, so a big change in vitamin K changes how well the drug works
why: It’s about vitamin K, which counteracts the drug.
hint: Which vitamin is needed to make clotting factors?
explain: Clotting factors need vitamin K to be made in their active form. Warfarin limits recycled vitamin K; a sudden surge of vitamin K from food overrides it and clotting goes up.

prompt:
A child with cystic fibrosis has thick mucus that blocks the pancreatic duct.

Why is the child given pancreatic enzyme capsules (pancrelipase) with every meal and snack?
choices: They replace the lipase, protease and amylase that can’t reach the intestine
They are vitamins that replace insulin
They denature mucus in the lungs
answer: They replace the lipase, protease and amylase that can’t reach the intestine
hint: What normally comes out of the pancreas into the intestine?
explain: Without pancreatic enzymes, fats and proteins aren’t digested (fatty stools, poor growth). The capsules supply the hydrolases with the food so digestion can happen.

prompt: A blood clot is held together by a mesh of the protein fibrin. In a stroke or heart attack, tPA may be given: it activates the zymogen plasminogen into plasmin, a protease. How does plasmin dissolve the clot?
choices: It acts as a vitamin that thickens the blood
It inhibits every protease in the blood
It joins fibrin strands together using ATP
It hydrolyzes peptide bonds in fibrin, breaking up the mesh
answer: It hydrolyzes peptide bonds in fibrin, breaking up the mesh
hint: Zymogen → active enzyme → what does it digest?
explain: Plasminogen is an inactive precursor (zymogen). tPA cuts it into active plasmin, which hydrolyzes the fibrin mesh and dissolves the clot.

prompt: Donepezil, used in Alzheimer’s disease, is a reversible inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down the nerve signal molecule acetylcholine. How does it help?
choices: It permanently inactivates every enzyme in the brain
Acetylcholine lasts longer at synapses, boosting weak nerve signals
It is a vitamin that rebuilds neurons
answer: Acetylcholine lasts longer at synapses, boosting weak nerve signals
hint: Less breakdown = more of the neurotransmitter.
explain: Slowing the enzyme that removes acetylcholine leaves more of it at the synapse. Unlike nerve agents, donepezil lets go, so the effect is controlled.

prompt: Statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin) look like the substrate of HMG-CoA reductase and bind its active site. They are
choices: Competitive inhibitors that lower cholesterol synthesis
Irreversible inhibitors that destroy the liver
Coenzymes that speed up cholesterol synthesis
answer: Competitive inhibitors that lower cholesterol synthesis
why: Statins compete and let go; they are reversible.
hint: Look-alike in the active site.
explain: HMG-CoA reductase controls the rate of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. A substrate look-alike in its active site slows the whole pathway.

prompt: The body breaks alcohol down in two steps: ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetate. Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, the enzyme for the second step. A person taking it drinks alcohol and becomes flushed and nauseated. Why?
choices: Acetaldehyde builds up because it can’t be oxidized to acetate
Ethanol builds up because it can’t be absorbed
answer: Acetaldehyde builds up because it can’t be oxidized to acetate
hint: Which step is blocked: the first or the second?
explain: Ethanol → acetaldehyde (alcohol dehydrogenase) → acetate (aldehyde dehydrogenase). Blocking the second step lets toxic acetaldehyde accumulate. Metronidazole can cause a similar reaction, so patients are told to avoid alcohol.

prompt: Aspirin and ibuprofen both block the enzyme COX. Aspirin transfers an acetyl group onto COX’s active site; ibuprofen sits in the active site without bonding to it. What is the key difference?
choices: Ibuprofen is a coenzyme for COX
Only aspirin is an enzyme inhibitor
Ibuprofen is irreversible; aspirin is reversible
Aspirin bonds covalently (irreversible); ibuprofen binds and lets go (reversible)
answer: Aspirin bonds covalently (irreversible); ibuprofen binds and lets go (reversible)
why: It’s the other way around: aspirin transfers an acetyl group onto COX.
hint: Which one forms a covalent bond?
explain: Aspirin acetylates a serine in COX, a permanent covalent change. Ibuprofen competes for the active site and leaves, so its effect wears off in hours.

prompt: Some bacteria make β-lactamase, which hydrolyzes penicillin. Augmentin adds clavulanic acid to amoxicillin. What does the clavulanic acid do?
choices: It inhibits β-lactamase so the antibiotic isn’t destroyed
It kills bacteria by denaturing them
It is a coenzyme for amoxicillin
answer: It inhibits β-lactamase so the antibiotic isn’t destroyed
hint: Protect the antibiotic from the enzyme that breaks it.
explain: β-lactamase is a bacterial hydrolase that breaks penicillin’s ring. Clavulanic acid binds it and permanently inactivates it, protecting the amoxicillin.

prompt: Normal blood pH is kept between 7.35 and 7.45. Why can severe acidosis (pH 7.0) be life-threatening?
choices: Enzymes are not affected by blood pH
Enzymes are pushed away from their optimum pH, changing the charges in their active sites
Acid makes enzymes work too fast
answer: Enzymes are pushed away from their optimum pH, changing the charges in their active sites
hint: Enzymes have an optimum pH.
explain: The charges on acidic and basic side chains depend on pH. Outside the normal range, enzymes lose activity and can denature, so buffers and breathing tightly control blood pH.

prompt: Allopurinol treats gout. It resembles the substrate of xanthine oxidase and slows uric acid production. It is
why: It looks like the substrate and binds the active site: competitive.
hint: Substrate look-alike = ?
explain: Allopurinol is a substrate look-alike for xanthine oxidase, so less uric acid forms and fewer painful crystals deposit in joints.

prompt: Omeprazole (a proton pump inhibitor) permanently blocks the pump that puts H+ into the stomach. What happens to pepsin activity?
choices: It stays the same; pH doesn’t affect enzymes
It increases, because pepsin likes a higher pH
It decreases, because the stomach pH rises above pepsin’s optimum of 2
answer: It decreases, because the stomach pH rises above pepsin’s optimum of 2
why: Pepsin’s optimum is pH 2; less acid moves it away from that.
hint: Pepsin’s optimum pH is…
explain: Less acid means a higher stomach pH. Pepsin works best near pH 2, so its activity drops, and pepsinogen is also activated less.

prompt: Methotrexate resembles folate and binds the active site of an enzyme needed to make DNA bases. It is a
choices: Coenzyme that speeds up DNA synthesis
Competitive inhibitor that slows dividing cells
answer: Competitive inhibitor that slows dividing cells
why: It blocks the folate enzyme; it does not help it.
hint: Folate look-alike = ?
explain: Rapidly dividing cells (cancer cells) need lots of DNA building blocks. A folate look-alike in the active site slows them down. Patients may be given a form of folate afterward to protect healthy cells.

prompt: Insulin is made as proinsulin, and enzymes cut out a section of the chain to activate it. Proinsulin is an example of a
choices: Zymogen (inactive precursor) activated by covalent modification
answer: Zymogen (inactive precursor) activated by covalent modification
hint: Inactive form, switched on by cutting.
explain: Proinsulin is inactive until peptidases break peptide bonds to remove the connecting piece (C-peptide). C-peptide levels can even be measured to check how much insulin a patient makes.

prompt:
A patient’s temperature is 41.5 °C (106.7 °F).

Why is a very high fever dangerous at the level of enzymes?
choices: Enzymes start to denature and lose their active sites
Enzymes speed up too much and run out of substrate
answer: Enzymes start to denature and lose their active sites
why: Above about 40 °C the bigger risk is unfolding, not speed.
hint: What does heat do to tertiary structure?
explain: Heat breaks the weak attractions that hold enzymes in shape. Above about 40–41 °C, important proteins begin to denature, which is why very high fevers are treated urgently.

prompt: Many glucose meter strips use glucose oxidase. Why does the strip give a reading for glucose and not for other sugars?
choices: Glucose is the only sugar in blood that dissolves
All sugars have the same shape
The enzyme is highly specific for glucose
answer: The enzyme is highly specific for glucose
hint: Which property of enzymes makes them good detectors?
explain: Enzyme specificity: glucose oxidase’s active site fits glucose. The reaction (glucose + O<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub> → gluconolactone + H<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub>O<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub>) makes a signal the meter reads.

prompt: ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) makes angiotensin II, a hormone that narrows blood vessels. Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor, lowers blood pressure. What does it do?
choices: It activates a zymogen that raises blood pressure
It blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, so less of the vessel-tightening hormone is made
It adds a vitamin cofactor to the heart
answer: It blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, so less of the vessel-tightening hormone is made
hint: The drug name tells you: ACE inhibitor.
explain: ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which narrows blood vessels. Inhibiting ACE lowers angiotensin II and blood pressure. A common side effect is a dry cough.

prompt: After cardiac arrest, a patient may be cooled to about 33–36 °C. How does lowering body temperature help?
choices: Cold raises the activation energy of every reaction
Enzyme-catalyzed reactions slow down, lowering the brain’s demand for oxygen
answer: Enzyme-catalyzed reactions slow down, lowering the brain’s demand for oxygen
why: Cooling slows enzymes; it does not denature them.
hint: Colder molecules collide less often.
explain: Lower temperature = fewer, slower collisions, so metabolism slows. Cells need less oxygen while the brain recovers.

prompt:
A patient takes a statin each morning with a large glass of grapefruit juice. Grapefruit contains compounds that inhibit CYP3A4, an enzyme in the intestinal wall that breaks down many drugs, including some statins.

What happens to the amount of statin that reaches the blood?
choices: It stays the same, because enzymes don’t act on drugs
It rises, because less of the drug is broken down on the way in
It falls, because grapefruit speeds up the enzyme
It falls, because grapefruit acid denatures the statin
answer: It rises, because less of the drug is broken down on the way in
why: Grapefruit inhibits the enzyme, so less drug is broken down: levels go up.
hint: If the breakdown enzyme is blocked, what happens to the drug level?
explain: Compounds in grapefruit inactivate CYP3A4 in the gut wall. Less of the drug is broken down on the way in, so more reaches the blood, raising the risk of side effects such as muscle damage.

prompt: Lab analyzers measure enzyme activity at a fixed temperature (37 °C) and in a buffer. Why?
choices: Temperature has no effect on enzymes
Buffers denature the enzymes so they can be counted
Enzyme activity changes with temperature and pH, so they must be kept constant to compare results
answer: Enzyme activity changes with temperature and pH, so they must be kept constant to compare results
hint: Which conditions change an enzyme’s rate?
explain: Rate depends on temperature, pH and substrate. With substrate in excess and temperature and pH fixed, the rate is proportional to how much enzyme is in the sample.

prompt:
Where these are found: CK, in skeletal muscle and heart muscle; troponin (a protein), in heart muscle only.

Lab reportPatient: 24-year-old, dark urine and sore muscles after an extreme workout
TestResultFlag
Creatine kinase (CK)↑↑↑HIGH
Troponinin rangenormal
What does the very high CK with normal troponin suggest?
choices: Skeletal muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis), not heart damage
answer: Skeletal muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis), not heart damage
why: Troponin is normal, so the heart is not the source.
hint: Which tissue has the most CK?
explain: CK is abundant in skeletal muscle. Extreme exercise, crush injuries or (rarely) statin side effects can break muscle down, releasing CK. Nurses push fluids to protect the kidneys.

prompt:
Where these enzymes are found: ALT and AST, mostly in liver cells; amylase, in the pancreas and salivary glands; CK, in muscle.

Lab reportPatient: 32-year-old, yellow skin, tired
TestResultFlag
ALT↑↑HIGH

Amylasein rangenormal

why: CK is normal. ALT and AST are concentrated in liver cells.
hint: ALT and AST: think liver.
explain: ALT and AST are aminotransferases concentrated in liver cells. Hepatitis, heavy alcohol use or an acetaminophen overdose releases them into the blood.

prompt:
Lab reportPatient: 58-year-old with crushing chest pain
TestResultFlag
Troponin↑↑HIGH
Creatine kinase (CK-MB)↑HIGH
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)↑HIGH
ALTin rangenormal
Why are CK and LDH higher in this patient’s blood?
choices: The enzymes were denatured by the injury
The liver released them to dissolve the clot
The heart made extra enzymes to repair itself
Damaged heart-muscle cells leaked their enzymes into the blood
answer: Damaged heart-muscle cells leaked their enzymes into the blood
hint: Where do these enzymes normally live?
explain: CK and LDH work inside cells. High activity in plasma means cell membranes broke open. (Troponin, the main heart test today, is a muscle protein, not an enzyme.)

prompt: In an enzyme test, extra substrate is added to the patient’s blood sample. Why use excess substrate?
choices: It makes the reaction release more energy
Then the rate depends only on how much enzyme is present
answer: Then the rate depends only on how much enzyme is present
why: Substrate doesn’t denature enzymes.
hint: Rate vs enzyme concentration with excess substrate is a straight line.
explain: With every active site saturated, the rate is at its maximum for that amount of enzyme. Doubling the enzyme doubles the rate, so the rate measures the enzyme level.

prompt:
Where these enzymes are found: lipase, in the pancreas; amylase, in the pancreas and salivary glands; ALT, mostly in liver cells.

Lab reportPatient: 45-year-old, severe upper-belly pain after heavy drinking
TestResultFlag
Lipase↑↑↑HIGH
Amylase↑↑HIGH
ALTin rangenormal
Which condition do these results suggest?
hint: Which organ makes lipase?
explain: The pancreas makes lipase and amylase. When it is inflamed, they leak into the blood. In pancreatitis, trypsin can also activate too early and digest the pancreas itself.

prompt:
Where these enzymes are found: ALP, in bone-building cells and the liver; ALT and AST, mostly in liver cells.

Lab reportPatient: 14-year-old during a growth spurt
TestResultFlag
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)↑HIGH
ALTin rangenormal
ASTin rangenormal
Which is the most likely explanation for the high ALP?
choices: Normal bone growth: bone-building cells release ALP
answer: Normal bone growth: bone-building cells release ALP
why: ALT and AST are normal, so the liver is fine.
hint: Teens are growing…
explain: ALP comes from bone and the liver (bile ducts). Teens growing quickly normally have higher ALP. With normal ALT and AST, bone is the likely source.

prompt: PSA (prostate-specific antigen), a common screening test, is actually a protease made by the prostate. A protease is a
why: Proteases break peptide bonds with water.
hint: -ase that acts on protein.
explain: PSA cuts proteins in semen. Higher blood levels can come from prostate enlargement, inflammation or cancer, so it is followed up with other tests.

prompt:
Where these enzymes are found: amylase, in the pancreas and salivary glands; lipase, in the pancreas.

Lab reportPatient: 9-year-old with swollen cheeks near the jaw (mumps)
TestResultFlag
Amylase↑HIGH
Lipasein rangenormal
Why is amylase high but lipase normal?
choices: Inflamed salivary glands release salivary amylase, but they don’t make lipase
Lipase was denatured in the sample
Amylase and lipase are the same enzyme
answer: Inflamed salivary glands release salivary amylase, but they don’t make lipase
why: Pancreatic damage would raise lipase too.
hint: Which of the two enzymes do salivary glands make?
explain: Amylase comes from both the pancreas and the salivary glands, so it is less specific. Lipase points to the pancreas. This is why lipase is the preferred pancreatitis test.

prompt:
A patient with long-term heavy alcohol use is confused and unsteady. Heavy drinking often causes a vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, so thiamine is given right away.

Which coenzyme is the patient short of?
why: FAD is made from riboflavin (B2). Thiamine becomes thiamine pyrophosphate.
hint: The coenzyme name hides the vitamin name: thiamine → thiamine ___.
explain: Thiamine (B1) is made into thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the coenzyme for enzymes that remove CO<sub style="font-size:11.3152px;line-height:17.5386px">2</sub> from pyruvate (decarboxylation). The brain depends on these energy-producing reactions, so a B1 deficiency (beriberi; in heavy drinkers, Wernicke encephalopathy) causes confusion and unsteadiness.

prompt:
Tyrosinase is the first enzyme of the pathway that turns the amino acid tyrosine into melanin, the pigment of skin, hair and eyes. In albinism, tyrosinase doesn’t work.

Why does the person make very little melanin, even with plenty of tyrosine?
choices: Melanin is a vitamin that must come from food
The first enzyme is missing, so tyrosine can’t be converted
Extra tyrosine denatures the skin’s proteins
Tyrosine is a competitive inhibitor of melanin
answer: The first enzyme is missing, so tyrosine can’t be converted
hint: What happens to a pathway when its first enzyme is missing?
explain: An enzyme pathway stops at the missing enzyme: without tyrosinase, tyrosine is not turned into melanin, so skin, hair and eyes lack pigment and sun protection is important.

prompt: The body breaks alcohol down in two steps: ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetate. Some people flush and feel sick after a small amount of alcohol because aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2), the enzyme for the second step, is weak. What builds up?
why: Ethanol is converted normally; the second step is slow.
hint: Which molecule does aldehyde dehydrogenase remove?
explain: Ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetate. A slow second enzyme lets acetaldehyde accumulate, causing flushing and nausea (the same effect disulfiram causes on purpose).

prompt:
An older adult has anemia, numb feet and memory problems (nerve damage). Their stomach no longer makes intrinsic factor, a protein needed to absorb one particular vitamin.

Which vitamin can’t be absorbed?
why: Folate deficiency causes anemia too, but intrinsic factor and nerve damage point to B12.
hint: Intrinsic factor + nerve damage.
explain: B12 needs intrinsic factor from the stomach to be absorbed. Without it: pernicious anemia and nerve damage. B12 is given by injection to bypass the gut.

prompt: A patient takes very large doses of vitamin A supplements for months. Why is this riskier than large doses of vitamin C?
choices: Vitamin A is water-soluble and is lost too fast
Both are flushed out in urine
Vitamin C is fat-soluble and is stored
Vitamin A is fat-soluble and is stored, so it can build up to toxic levels
answer: Vitamin A is fat-soluble and is stored, so it can build up to toxic levels
why: Vitamin A is one of the fat-soluble four (A, D, E, K).
hint: ADEK are stored.
explain: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in fat tissue and the liver, so excess accumulates. Extra water-soluble vitamins (B and C) are mostly lost in urine.

prompt:
A newborn screen shows very high phenylalanine.

The baby lacks phenylalanine hydroxylase, the enzyme that breaks down the amino acid phenylalanine (PKU). The sweetener aspartame is a dipeptide of aspartic acid and phenylalanine. Why must the baby avoid aspartame?
choices: Aspartame is a vitamin they lack
Aspartame contains phenylalanine, which they can’t break down and which damages the brain
answer: Aspartame contains phenylalanine, which they can’t break down and which damages the brain
hint: What is aspartame made from?
explain: Without the enzyme, phenylalanine builds up and harms brain development. A low-phenylalanine diet started early prevents this, which is why diet sodas carry a “Phenylketonurics: contains phenylalanine” warning.

prompt: In Tay-Sachs disease, a hydrolase that normally breaks down gangliosides (sphingolipids in nerve-cell membranes) is missing. What happens?
choices: A lipid (ganglioside) that should be broken down builds up in nerve cells
Glucose builds up in the blood
answer: A lipid (ganglioside) that should be broken down builds up in nerve cells
hint: A missing hydrolase means its substrate…
explain: Without this hydrolase, gangliosides aren’t broken down in lysosomes and accumulate in neurons, causing progressive nerve damage.

prompt:
A toddler living in an older home has anemia, belly pain and trouble concentrating. Old paint is peeling.

Lead (Pb2+) causes anemia by inhibiting enzymes that make heme for hemoglobin. How does it inhibit them?
choices: It binds their –SH groups and stays bound (irreversible, noncompetitive)
It acts as a coenzyme that makes the enzymes work too fast
It looks like iron, competes for the active site and wears off
answer: It binds their –SH groups and stays bound (irreversible, noncompetitive)
why: Lead binds tightly to –SH groups; it doesn’t simply compete and leave.
hint: Heavy metals bind –SH groups.
explain: Heavy metals such as Pb<sup style="font-size:10.3168px;line-height:15.991px">2+</sup> bind sulfhydryl groups on enzymes (including ones in the heme pathway), irreversibly and noncompetitively. Less heme means less hemoglobin: anemia. Chelating drugs pull the lead off.

prompt: Why are people who could become pregnant advised to take folic acid (B9) before and during early pregnancy?
choices: It prevents scurvy in the baby
Its coenzyme (THF) is needed to make DNA bases for rapidly dividing cells, preventing neural-tube defects
It is stored in fat and can’t be lost
It is a heavy metal that protects the baby
answer: Its coenzyme (THF) is needed to make DNA bases for rapidly dividing cells, preventing neural-tube defects
hint: Which coenzyme helps build DNA bases?
